Trump Can’t Even Make the Planes Run On Time

The clown show would be funny if it weren’t dangerous.

William Kristol, Andrew Egger, Jim Swift

READ TO ME

Donald Trump is off to Asia. The president touched down in the Philippines this morning for the first leg of a four-day trip that will include a pair of international summits and a long-expected trilateral meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. Amazingly, Trump continues to suggest he doesn’t even think the war in Ukraine will be worth raising at that summit—but we imagine Putin will find some creative ways to slip the topic in. Happy Tuesday.

(Photo illustration by Sarah Rogers/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty)

Culture War Is Easy. Governing Is Hard.

by Andrew Egger

In theory, America’s massively outdated air traffic control systems are exactly the sort of problem Donald Trump’s voters put him in office to fix: a longstanding bureaucratic issue that had been kicked down the road for years, where a hard-charging, no-bullshit innovator could cut through the inertia and, with an assist from his buds in the tech world, get some real stuff done.

But since Friday’s airport chaos, Trump and co. have once again reminded us that they’re particularly bad at this sort of work. Real governing, it turns out, is boring, hard work—work that Trump is too flighty, too distractible, too obsessed with quick fixes, and too obsessed with blaming Democrats to make headway on.

Here’s something Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy are right about: Neither the current state of our ATC infrastructure nor Friday’s outage was squarely the administration’s fault. The current communications systems are astonishingly old and rickety, built on decades-old infrastructure that is sometimes so obsolete that nobody manufactures replacement parts anymore. Governments everywhere are famously slow to upgrade software and hardware systems; that “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” approach seems particularly attractive when it comes to a nationwide communications system that runs 24/7 with zero downtime. And legislative efforts to overhaul and modernize the system have often run aground.

And to his credit, Duffy has had his eye on the problem. He brought up the need to modernize our aviation systems in his confirmation hearing last year, and has spent the time since lobbying for billions of dollars to modernize ATC specifically. Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion to the problem.

But the administration hasn’t gotten that money all out. And now Duffy says he needs even more. He insisted Friday that another $50 billion is needed, while blaming Democrats for the holdup: “How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?” A reporter noted that Republicans have had full control of D.C. for two years. “Oftentimes you need a bipartisan vote,” Duffy replied.

Except that isn’t even true in this case. The One Big Beautiful Bill was a party-line reconciliation package. If Duffy and the White House had wanted to try to convince Republican lawmakers to throw a few more billions at ATC modernization there, they could have done so.

The reason they didn’t is straightforward: because as much as Duffy wants to rewrite the record, this problem simply hasn’t been a major priority for Trump himself.

The president made that very clear yesterday when he clownishly tried to palm the whole problem off on his predecessor: “The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass.” But “hooking up copper into glass”—gradually replacing antiquated copper-wire systems with fiber-optic cable, in other words—is part of the modernization and maintenance effort that Duffy is begging for funds to continue. This was the exact work that a government contractor was doing Friday—not under orders from Joe Biden!—when the error arose that caused the ground stop. Wake the president up when it’s time to cover the radar towers with gold leaf.

Are you stuck in an airport, looking for something to listen to or read? The Bulwark has you covered.

Join

Trump was far from opposed to making sweeping tech changes to the government when he came back into office last year. But his focus wasn’t on boring maintenance like ATC. It was on high-conflict, high-violence culture-war projects like Elon Musk’s DOGE that, if anything, set the FAA back: Hundreds of FAA employees took DOGE’s “fork in the road” offer for early-retirement buyouts, shrinking an already stressed workforce, and conversations about ATC modernization last year were dominated by concerns that Musk would use his influence with Trump to barge in and nab the contract for Starlink.

So Republicans missed their first chances to deal with ATC modernization under Trump 2.0, not because Biden left them in too big a hole or because they had to deal with furries flying planes first, but because they just didn’t care.

Now that it’s back in the headlines, they have to care. But that requires actual interest in the nitty gritty of governing. It requires grunt work that doesn’t actually generate headlines. It requires reaching across the aisle to strike a deal.

Can they do it? It’s possible—but if it happens, it will be more in spite of the administration than because of it. Bipartisan compromise requires constructive, respectful negotiation, and these guys just can’t turn the culture-war mode off: In an interview last night, Vice President JD Vance said that Republicans could absolutely strike a deal with Democrats “if they set to side their ridiculous obsession with men in women’s sports.”

And it’s not obvious Trump even wants to try. After all, this is hard work. Shouldn’t we maybe just count our blessings that things aren’t even more broken than they are? “It’s life,” the president said this morning when asked about a series of major tech outages this week. “When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

Congress: Stand With Ukraine. Speak for America.

by William Kristol

President Trump plans to meet in Shenzhen Thursday with two of his favorite dictators, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. (It may become a trio of tyrants, if North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, as Trump hopes, joins the devil’s banquet.) Attention will understandably be focused on Xi Jinping in light of the China chips scandal engulfing the Trump administration. But what about Putin, the man who’s been Trump’s buddy for even longer than Xi?

Trump has repeatedly tried over the last two years to rehabilitate Putin. He’s worked consistently to bring him in from the diplomatic and economic cold into which he was justly consigned after his invasion of Ukraine. And Putin has responded by intensifying his war. As the New York Times summarized yesterday, “Trump Has Eased Up on Russia, but Russia Hasn’t Eased Up on Ukraine.”

Even as the Trump administration has offered Moscow sanctions relief, energy deals and warm words this fall, Russia has been escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities in some of the deadliest attacks against civilians in years.

And yet, Trump said last month that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine.” The U.S. president excuses—no, he supports—Russia’s brutal aggression against its democratic neighbor. This is a source of shame for this country.

What can be done? Well, as I wrote yesterday,

The leaders of the next Congress could say, loudly and clearly, to both our adversaries and our allies, that not just the president but Congress represents the United States of America. And that while President Trump can say what he wants this week in Asia, Congress intends to act forcefully over the next two years to establish policies in accord with our national interests and principles.

Our elected representatives in Congress can make clear, now, this week, today, that our current president does not speak for the American people. They can deplore Trump’s statements and condemn his actions. And Democratic leaders can commit to reversing them as soon as possible in the new Congress—pledging to restore sanctions and pass an aid package for Ukraine in January, and committing to working to override a Trump veto on either.

Then again, why wait until January? Many Republicans in Congress claim to be on the side of Ukraine, not Putin. Bipartisan legislation to restore sanctions on Russia and to help Ukraine could be passed in the current lame-duck Congress. The legislative process could begin this week.

Congress can’t stop Trump from saying what he’ll say in China. But Congress can make clear that Trump speaks only for Trump. Congress can speak and act for America.

QUICK HITS

CHIPS FOR CHINA: Donald Trump spent much of this year scoffing off concerns about rapidly accelerating AI development. Any deliberate slowing of the pace of new models, the president has said, is unacceptable: All that matters is staying ahead of China in the race to AI superintelligence.

This is an irresponsible posture on its face. But what’s become shockingly clear during the Nvidia scandal is how insanely the White House has behaved even according to its own theory of AI development—by repeatedly refusing to take enforcement and policy steps that would keep China from immediately helping itself to America’s AI gains.

It isn’t just that Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department was asleep at the switch when it came to keeping tabs on the advanced AI chips Nvidia sold to shell companies in Southeast Asia (and that subsequently turned up in Chinese labs). The Trump White House also deliberately made it easier for China to access cutting-edge chips without having to import them at all.

If Chinese companies can’t get their hands on Nvidia’s most modern chips themselves, the next best thing is for them to rent access to them from data centers in nearby third countries not subject to the same export controls. This practice, known as “remote access,” obviously helps China skirt America’s chip controls, but it also creates highly lucrative new markets for Nvidia to sell its chips. Which may explain why the White House, after tearing up Biden-era regulations designed to clamp down on remote access, never got around to issuing new ones.

Until yesterday, that is, when the Commerce Department released an emergency rule “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

Remarkably, a press release made it clear the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council.” Even now, Lutnick seems reluctant to crack down on the Nvidia-China relationship without somebody twisting his arm.

WOKE IS BACK: The Trump administration really wants to be able to tell public universities what they are and aren’t allowed to research. But federal courts have so far stymied their attempts to do so. And yesterday, the Supreme Court refused to ride to the administration’s aid. Here’s Politico:

The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a petition from the Trump administration to review a temporary block on its effort to cut millions of dollars in research grants to University of California researchers over diversity-related language.

Monday’s denial leaves a lower court ruling in favor of the researchers intact. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in May found the terminations likely violated the First Amendment and blocked the administration from canceling the grants while the case is ongoing. Justices offered no explanation for declining review.

The Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to resolve whether the First Amendment prohibits the government from considering the viewpoints advanced by academic research when awarding or terminating competitive grants. The administration also argued it has broad discretion to determine which projects receive taxpayer funding.

Productiv-icky

Digging holes on the beach

Ben Tossell

Nov 17

READ IN APP

productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do

We have a problem.

full interactive post is here

We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them.

So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy.

But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend…

Yeses are easy. They’re quick.

But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes.

Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about.

I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate.

I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master.

Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine.

Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is.

We started measuring shovels instead of the hole.

Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff.

You feel behind. Like way behind.

So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with.

Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole.

I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom.

But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot.

Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole?

Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse.

8 America’s EV boom is happening without car buyers

Delivery fleets, robotaxis, and police cars are going electric. (Atlantic $)

9 New cosmic data has challenged our model of the universe

The findings suggest dark energy may be weakening. (Quanta)

10 A Buddhist sect plans to build an AI guru for Silicon Valley

It wants to create a model based on a collective mind. (New Yorker $)

Quote of the day

“Export controls 2.0 is here.”

—Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, tells Reuters that Washington has opened a new front in its campaign to slow China's AI ambitions.

One more thing

Welcome to Kenya’s Great Carbon Valley: a bold new gamble to fight climate change

Kenya’s Great Rift Valley is home to five geothermal power stations, which harness clouds of steam to generate about a quarter of the country’s electricity. But some of the energy escapes into the atmosphere, while even more remains underground for lack of demand. That’s what brought Octavia Carbon here.

Last year, the startup began harnessing some of that excess energy to remove CO2 from the air. The company says the method is efficient, affordable, and—crucially—scalable. But the project also faces fierce opposition.

Read the full story on the future of Kenya’s "Great Carbon Valley."

—Diana Kruzman

Taiwan Elections Show What the People Really Care About

Guest post from Tim Culpan: China barely factors, as local issues like housing, employment and public safety drive voter choice

Tim Culpan

Nov 17

Guest post

READ IN APP

This is guest post from Tim Culpan, a journalist and 27-year Taipei resident. Tim worked for Bloomberg News as the Taipei technology correspondent and then opinion columnist until 2024, when he went independent and launched the excellent Culpium on Substack. I am a subscriber and he pitched me on a piece about the November 28 Taiwan municipal elections I thought it could be useful for Sinocism readers. Let us know what you think in the comments, and do check out more of Tim’s work over at Culpium. - Bill

Good Evening from Taipei,

A few weeks ago I pitched to Bill the idea of writing a piece for Sinocism about the November 28 Taiwan municipal elections. City and county mayors will be elected, along with thousands of other local representatives. It’s not a nationwide poll.

“It’s a plebiscite on local issues,” I told him.

My reason for publishing through Sinocism, instead of my own outlet Culpium is that Sinocism is the premier foreign destination for discussion on China politics and policy. I could foresee that many people would mistake this local Taiwanese election as some kind of referendum on Taiwan’s China policy.

I recognize the irony of publishing a piece arguing that Taiwan’s election is not about China in a publication focused on China. But by explaining the nuances of Taiwanese domestic issues, my hope is that China watchers will understand how and why citizens in this democracy make decisions. Quite often these decisions appear counter to what outsiders feel should be the wise & logical choice vis-a-vis Beijing.

Sinocism readers seem like the perfect audience for such a discussion, and I am grateful to Bill for lending me your ears.

One Election; 11,000 Positions

Taiwan has 23 million people, 19.7 million voters, and 22 cities and counties. Candidates are vying for four-year terms and can serve a maximum of two terms. Victory is determined by a first-past-the-post system with no preferences and no postal or electronic voting. Whomever gets the most votes from in-person voting wins, even if it’s not a majority.

Among the seats to be filled are mayors (city), magistrates (county), and municipal councilors.

Yet Taiwan’s administrative divisions get even smaller, like Russian nesting dolls, all the way down to local villages and neighborhoods (also called wards or burroughs). All up, 11,051 seats are to be filled, and village chiefs (村長 - cunzhang) plus neighborhood captains (里長 - lizhang) will account for more than 7,700 of those positions.

The largest electorate to be served by this election is New Taipei City with 4 million residents, the smallest being Rongxin Village in Nantou County with just 36 souls.

My point is that this really is local. Super local. As a result, policy focus is on local rather than national issues.

All Politics is Local

What voters care about most varies by region. In the north (Taipei, Keelung, Taoyuan), housing and urban renewal is a key concern, alongside transport and public safety. In the center (Taichung, Changhua), food scandals and public health predominate. While in the south (Tainan, Kaohsiung), wages and flood control are particularly local topics.

This regional variation dilutes the value of national-level policies and reduces the importance of broad party platforms. As a result, the Kuomintang’s (KMT) perceived pro-business reputation carries less weight while the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) old-school social justice platform is getting fresh oxygen.

To be clear, it shouldn’t be taken as fact that the KMT is pro-business and the DPP is pro-social. There’s plenty of evidence to suggest the reverse is sometimes true. Yet, the basic ideological divide persists in the same way that the Tories and Labour occupy different sides of the UK political spectrum.

Taiwanese Taipei

Traditionally, Taichung in central Taiwan is seen as a “swing state” and barometer of changing political winds across the country. Taiwan’s geographical layout almost perfectly maps to its political layout. Taipei and New Taipei City in the North are deep blue (KMT) while Tainan and Kaohsiung in the South are deep green (DPP). These shades start to blend as you move toward Taiwan’s geographic center.

This year, however, something extraordinary is happening.

Taipei City, the national capital and seat of economic power, may change colors. The KMT’s Chiang Wan-an won the 2022 mayoral election, but there’s a high chance he’ll lose his post this election.

Instead, polling shows that it’s likely the DPP will take Taipei City Hall for the first time since Chen Shui-bian’s single four-year term which spanned 1994-1998. (The “whites,” lead by independent populist Ko Wen-je, split the vote of the two major parties and took Taipei City from 2014 to 2022).

Surveys have them within a few points of each other, and the margin of error is such that I am not confident calling this race. Also, you won’t see new polls in the coming week because Taiwanese law prohibits them from being published in the 10 days leading up to an election.

Chiang is claimed to be a great grandson of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek through an extra-marital affair, with his family name enjoying the cachet that comes with such a connection. To his credit though, Chiang’s resume is impressive in its own right with academic credentials that culminate in a Juris Doctorate Degree (JD) from UPenn’s Carey Law School and admission to the California Bar.

City Vision

But voter’s adulation for Chiang is waning amid dissatisfaction over very local issues. Clean, efficient, and friendly on the surface, Taipei City is getting old. Vast tracts of its housing stock is over 30 years old with residential communities a stone’s throw from City Hall that are close to 50 years old (and which look every bit their age). At the same time, there’s a lack of new affordable housing coming on stream.

Urban renewal policies, which allow a building to be torn down and rebuilt if enough owners approve the measure, were supposed to ameliorate this problem. But the slow pace of new projects and the bureaucratic minefield involved with rehousing residents has caused great satisfaction among voters. Add to that a litany of small gripes like scooter parking, public smoking, traffic safety, and elder loneliness, and Chiang’s leadership has started to feel lacklustre in the eyes of many voters.

His challenger, Puma Shen of the DPP, has come out of the gate with a more polished vision for the city which he is pitching to voters under the slogan HEART (Habitat, Empower, Accompany, Resilience, Time). In truth, Shen’s policies aren’t vastly different to Chiang’s, but he’s successfully managed to stoke a renewed sense of pride among Taipei residents.

DPP’s Taipei Mayoral Candidate Puma Shen at a campaign rally with supporters, including President Lai Ching-te (immediately behind) and former president Tsai Ing-wen (behind, right). Photo: Puma Shen Campaign Office

Currently a national legislator, Shen is a former criminology professor who gained recognition for his research into Chinese disinformation and cognitive warfare against Taiwan. That career trajectory took him to founding Doublethink Lab focused on cognitive warfare and Kuma Academy which conducts research and training into urban resilience (read: preparing for war).

Perhaps surprisingly, Shen’s China-focused background has barely featured in this campaign. Clumsily, though, Beijing has managed to burnish his credentials through a series of operations aimed at surveilling and curtailing him.

Local Matters Matter

Elsewhere in Taiwan, national issues like macroeconomic policy, defense, and China relations have also taken a backseat. In fact, political leaders have been excoriated for pandering too much to national interests over local issues.

Outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen, for example, was once seen as a rising star within the KMT for her leadership in the this important benchmark city. Instead, she received significant backlash over her handling of a tainted cooking oil scandal in July this year. That incident comes eight months after Lu admitted that her administration mishandled an outbreak of African Swine Fever. Critics claim she cared more about the KMT’s national exposure than the concerns of her local constituents.

Elder Care, Traditional Industry

In central and southern Taiwan voters are honing in on specific issues, and candidates are adapting their policies to suit. Care for the elderly has become both an emotive and practical issue among families struggling to juggle work commitments with the burden of aged care. Wage disparity between traditional and tech industries is an acute problem outside the traditional tech belts (Hsinchu and Taipei) where old-school manufacturing industries dominate.

Because of the very local nature of each race, the results and implications of this nine-in-one local election will be difficult to parse. Although the ballot falls mid-way between the 2024 and 2028 presidential and legislative elections, this is not a mid-term election in the US sense.

It’s absolutely true that hard-core DPP and KMT supporters will make their choice regardless of the candidate or policies. But that loyalty is far weaker at the local level, making this much more a plebiscite on policies than party.

National Implications

That said, there are national implications, and China policy is a good case study.

I’d argue that in the US, guns are an issue of ideology not merely policy. And most voters do not choose a candidate based on ideology as long their ideologies are not vastly in conflict. Having the ‘correct’ position on guns won’t be enough to win a majority of votes, but having the ‘incorrect’ position might lose you an election. The best choice for a candidate is to just shut up and not talk about it

However, the factional nature of democratic systems means that losing an election on policy necessarily hampers your ability to control the conversation on ideology. That’s unless some external force — a mass shooting or missile crisis — puts that ideological discussion back on the front page.

Chiang Wan-an campaign poster. Photo: Chiang campaign office.

Taiwanese views on relations with China fit into a similar paradigm. It matters, but it doesn’t occupy their daily thoughts unless reminded. Local candidates have largely been smart enough to not talk about China and instead focus on more relevant issues.

If Chiang Wan-an loses Taipei City, it won’t be because of his China policy, and ergo it shouldn’t be seen as a challenge to Beijing or its leader Xi Jinping (XJP). If you come across a headline in foreign media which says this Taiwan election is a rebuke to China, then I implore you to cancel your subscription.

Ideological Control

Yet a DPP win will help the ruling party control the ideological debate against a KMT that’s struggled on the national level to offer anything beyond “all the way with XJP.”

KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun doesn’t appear smart enough to understand this reality. Her cozy-up-to-China policy won her support within the party because its leadership is stacked with pro-China hardliners, but it has alienated most of Taiwan, including thousands of KMT voters.

Read “War and Chips. And the KMT” at Culpium

Still, it appears to be the only policy Cheng has been able, or willing, to enunciate. In a briefing with the Taiwan Foreign Correspondents Club earlier this year, she waffled and dodged all manner of questions ranging from economics to semiconductor policy.

KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun speaks to the Taiwan Foreign Correspondents’ Club, 23 March 2026. Photo: Tim Culpan/Culpium

As a result of Cheng’s lack of policy depth in favor of stubbornly hewing to party ideology, some local KMT candidates have made the unusual decision of distancing themselves from the party Chair.

Like the GOP Losing Texas

It’s almost certain that Cheng will lose her Chairmanship should the KMT lose Taipei City because such a scenario would be akin to the GOP losing the Texas Governorship or Senate seat.

But her position is under threat even if Chiang holds on to Taipei City and the party loses other “safe” posts or simply loses ground across the more than 11,000 positions up for grabs. For example, the New Taipei City mayoralship which the KMT has held since 2005 has a very real chance of falling to the DPP.

If this happens, the ideological grasp which Cheng and her hardline supporters have over the KMT would weaken, ushering in a more conciliatory tone favored by younger party members. By this, I mean more readily embracing a Taiwan-first future for both the KMT and the nation, which would necessarily mean de-emphasising without fully abandoning its long-held China unification platform.

Beijing’s Finger on The Pulse

What this means for Xi Jinping and Beijing’s view of Taiwan, I can’t answer. Over the past 30 years, Taiwanese have de-emphasized the unification v independence debate in favor of real meat-and-potatoes issues like economics, public welfare, and living standards. Yet it seems to me, from my seat in Taipei, the Chinese Communist Party has been unable to keep up with this changing tone.

For a while, during the Ma Ying-jeou era of 2008-2016, it looked like Beijing got it: the way to Taiwanese hearts was through their wallets, and offering the economic benefits of close ties to China was a somewhat winning strategy.

The Sunflower Movement of 2014, coupled with Beijing’s crackdown on Hong Kong’s Umbrella Movement, and then the harshness of Covid have taught Taiwanese to distrust Beijing. From there, we’ve seen a continued disinformation campaign both overseas and domestically aimed at painting Taiwan’s economic future as bleak and its security future as hopeless.

Welcome to Find me at Culpium

I think this election will show that Taiwanese are not falling for it. They have real gripes, and electoral candidates across both sides of the political rainbow have stepped up to address those concerns. And as long as Taiwanese believe that their leaders are listening, acting, and improving then I think the constant barrage of disinformation will be increasingly ignored. I wish I could say the same for foreign observers who still cling to Beijing’s view of Taiwan.

Xi Jinping Thought

An interesting question I’d love to have answered is how Xi Jinping may act once he realises that Taiwanese are largely ignoring him as they focus on local issues. And that, my new Sinocism friends, is a topic I’ll let you all discuss.

Meanwhile, if you want to keep tabs on Taiwan, its technology sector, industrial development, and the Jensen Huang firestorm, then you’re welcome to come visit me over at Culpium.

Thanks for reading.

Tim

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

⚖️ California takes OpenAI to court over agent escapes

Image source: Office of the Attorney General of California

The Rundown: California Attorney General Rob Bonta just sued OpenAI over the company’s July incident, in which its AI agents hacked Hugging Face, arguing it came after weeks of missed warning signs and was one of 80+ times its test agents escaped.

The details:

Bonta says OpenAI dodged his office’s questions during a probe opened in September, with the suit marking the first by a state over the breach.

After agents crashed a shared tool on July 4, OpenAI resumed testing within days and missed the weeklong breakout entirely, the suit says.

California says only 27 agent escapes are public, though OpenAI admitted to over 80 and has notified dozens of outside targets, including a federal agency.

The state wants a court order forcing OpenAI to test more safely, plus $2,500 for each violation and any money it made from the misconduct.

Why it matters: Between the quietly growing number of escapes, rogue agent ‘swarms,’ and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening across the web. Though the Hugging Face incident feels like ancient history in AI time, the fallout from it is still far from over.

AI & GEOPOLITICS

🇺🇸 Trump set to crown AI ‘national champions’

Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown

The Rundown: The U.S. is reportedly set to label over two dozen U.S. AI firms, including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic, as “national champions,” with faster export approvals and financing to sell American AI abroad, coming in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

The details:

The designated “champions” could see U.S. officials advocating for them with foreign governments, a fast lane on chip export licenses, and federal financing.

The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers get U.S. chips, data centers, and AI models as a single bundle instead of turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

Commerce chief Howard Lutnick will reportedly announce the picks while facing accusations of ignoring warnings about a firm tied to chips reaching China.

Commenting on Huang, Pres. Trump said a return as Nvidia CEO is something he “would not mind,” though he still backs ex-Apple CEO Tim Cook for the position.

Why it matters: The Jensen fallout had officials pushing the U.S. toward tighter chip controls. Instead, Nvidia is still on the champions list, and Trump says he’d be fine with Jensen back. The White House clearly believes winning the AI race means selling more U.S. chips — an important position heading into Trump’s upcoming meeting with Xi.

AI TRAINING

🧠 Make your AI usage go further with these tips

The Rundown: Claude Pro's $20 plan runs on a five-hour and a weekly limit, and long chats and high-effort use both use it up faster. In this guide, you'll set up a leaner chat and have Claude ask you multiple-choice questions before it builds anything.

Step-by-step:

Click your account button at the bottom of Claude's sidebar, then Usage. Note when the Current session and weekly bars reset

In a new chat, click the model button under the chat box and set Effort to Low. Under + and Connectors, switch off apps the chat won't use

Prompt: “Don't start yet. I want to [task]. Ask me up to five smart multiple-choice questions about what I want. After that, sketch the plan and wait for my go-ahead”

Send your go-ahead and every change in one message. If a reply is missed, edit your message instead of sending a correction

When a chat runs long, ask for a handoff summary under 150 words and paste it into a new chat

Pro tip: Using another AI assistant? Skip the Claude settings and keep the habits. The sketch-first prompt, the one-message templates, and the handoff work in any chatbot.

OPENAI

🔬 OpenAI tracks how scientists really use ChatGPT

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists who used ChatGPT’s free academic pilot, with surveyed researchers saying AI lets them work ~2x faster at the same quality, coming as the company opens the program to up to 200K researchers.

The details:

Writing research code stood out, with scientists saying AI allowed them to work nearly 3x faster, and about 2x faster at brainstorming research ideas.

Scientists also leaned on AI for research ideas, with 23% of ideation requests asking ChatGPT to suggest a research question itself.

Scientists under 30 spent almost twice as much of their AI use on code as those aged 40+, while older users leaned on it more for teaching and admin.

OpenAI also announced an expansion of the free program, with applications for 50K first-come ChatGPT Plus grants opening on Nov. 23.

Why it matters: The AI-in-science hype train is frequently showing off the autonomous labs, thousand-agent swarms, and full AI scientists. But OpenAI’s data says the real use today is far more ordinary, with scientists using AI to read papers, draft writing, and generate code for experiments.

Hello,

Here are the five things you need to know today:

IRAN. Everything but the market signals escalation.

UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Kyiv and Brussels spoil Putin’s summit.

NORTH KOREA. If Kim travels, it will be to legitimise his bombs.

CHINA. Trump heads to Shenzhen as policy sails in the opposite direction.

UNITED STATES. The economy’s riskiest interdependency isn’t financial.

IRAN. Dirty look

Everything but the market signals escalation.

Iran was developing plans to use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington DC, CNN said Monday. A draft Department of Energy funding bill revealed the first new designation for a nuclear gravity bomb in decades, the B94.

INTELLIGENCE. The White House hasn’t denied the report, but it’s possible the Beltway brinksmanship is just deterrence by other means, or a way to show that Trump is considering all options while doing nothing. Oil markets, falling in tandem with stocks and other risk assets, seem to consider it all a TACO, as Iran continues to hit tankers and refuse nuclear inspections. Yet such indifference risks finding a smoking gun in the shape of a mushroom cloud.

FOR BUSINESS. Nuclear escalation remains remote for both sides, but as the n-word moves from the margins to the mainstream, the Overton window expands too. And while he’s held back since his midterm defeat, the availability of another aircraft carrier in CENTCOM’s region, plus the humiliation from Sunday’s 60 Minutes’ expose, gives Trump more impetus to strike. As he prepares to meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China, he won’t want to look weak.

UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Burning bridges

Kyiv and Brussels spoil Putin's summit.

Ukraine launched its biggest drone attack of the war, hitting Russia’s main bridge to Crimea and several oil refineries, as the EU expanded its sanctions list to include Russia’s richest woman. Russia targeted bridges and energy plants in Kyiv...

Ho Kan's Exhibition Opening This Week

Privacy for the Paranoid: The Ultimate Limits of Secrecy on December 2

View in browser

Dear Members and Friends,

I am delighted to announce the opening of Ho Kan: The World Opens Between Forms, a major international debut for post-war abstract artist Ho Kan (b. 1932), co-founder of Taiwan’s Ton-Fan Art Group who later spent 50 years in Milan. The exhibition runs from November 21, 2026, to February 21, 2027, and opens with a symposium on November 21 featuring curator Nataline Colonnello, Hsiao Chong-ray, Chris Wan, and other distinguished art historians, scholars, and curators, with simultaneous interpretation in English and Mandarin. Curator Nataline Colonnello will lead a tour for members on November 23.

Beyond the exhibition, India by the Bay returns to Asia Society Hong Kong Center for its 11th year. “Heritage, Reimagined” celebrates the richness and creativity of Indian culture with a vibrant lineup spanning music, dance, theater, literature, cinema, textiles, and fashion. Highlights include author, columnist, and entrepreneur Twinkle Khanna; India’s Ambassador to China, Mr. Vikram Doraiswami; and the Keelaka Dance Company. Reserve your spot now!

Can quantum science redefine secrecy? On December 2, the Hang Lung Mathematics Awards return to the Center for a conversation with Professors Artur Ekert and Giulio Chiribella on how quantum science is reshaping secure communication—and challenging our understanding of trust, privacy, and secrecy. The conversation continues over an exclusive dinner with Mr. Ronnie C. Chan. Explore the lineup and register below.

As part of Asia Society Hong Kong's educational series, Learners to Leaders and Junior Discovery Series continue to offer enriching experiences for young minds. This year-long program encourages students to learn and have fun beyond the classroom, exploring diverse topics that promote creativity, foster critical thinking, and enhance environmental awareness. Last week, our young learners immersed themselves in the beauty of music. They explored Beethoven’s works through band and orchestral music, and attended an unforgettable concert featuring VOCES8.

Coming up next: Sustainable Foundry Workshop on December 12. Seats fill up fast—interested students can book their spot via the ELA portal HERE.

We’d be glad to welcome you to our Center, whether you come along to a program or simply drop by to see what’s on.

Sincerely,

S. Alice Mong

REGISTER NOW

Ho Kan: The World Opens Between Forms

November 21, 2026 - February 21, 2027

Asia Society Hong Kong Center is pleased to present Ho Kan: The World Opens Between Forms, which brings the work of 94-year-old postwar geometric abstract master Ho Kan (霍剛, b. 1932) to Hong Kong for his first institutional solo-presentation in the city. Through 70 artworks and never-before-seen archival and personal materials from the newly-launched Ho Kan Art Archive, this exhibition offers a comprehensive retrospective of Ho's artistic evolution over his seven decades, tracing his role in co-founding Taiwan's pioneering Ton Fan Group and his fifty years in Milan’s avant-garde art world.

Drawing from private collections across the Asia Pacific region, this exhibition iscurated by guest curator Nataline Colonnello, with specialist consultant Felix Kwok,and support provided by the Asia Society Hong Kong Center Gallery & Exhibitions Team, Chris Wan, Hain Yoon, and Brynn Gordon.

Putin’s preposterous proposals are no path to peace

Putin’s preposterous proposals are no path to peace. Putin’s preposterous proposals are no path to peace fanny.pollet@i… Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:00 5 minutes The talks in Abu Dhabi produced no diplomatic breakthrough. Nor is one likely before winter, as Russia seeks to use the intervening months both to weaken Ukraine and to raise the cost of supporting Kyiv for its partners. Instead of showing any readiness to compromise, as the increasingly impatient US negotiators taken in by the prospect of lucrative business deals dangled before them by Russia’s rainmaker-in-chief Kirill Dmitrev had hoped, Russia succeeded in placing a future European security architecture on the table. The EU should recognise Russia’s renewed ‘interest’ in the European security architecture for what it is: an attempt to sow discord. Moscow’s intent? To portray the alleged failure of the European security system as the ‘explanation’ for the war, rather than its own imperial ambitions; to keep the Americans busy talking and limit their involvement in efforts to contain Russia; and, crucially, to confront Europeans with a dilemma. The latter do not wish to renegotiate existing security institutions but may fear that, unless they get involved, the basic contours of a new architecture may be negotiated over their heads before they muster the strength and resolve to stand their ground. An architecture of Russia’s aggression Electricity in Kyiv is already available for only a few hours a day at best, and the population now has to contend with water shortages as well. Why would Russia reduce the pressure now, when it can hold out for the possibility of a new political landscape emerging in Europe next year, hoping that these two factors will combine to force Ukraine to sue for an unfavourable peace? . But that is precisely the point: Russia is not interested in peace. Instead, it deploys diplomacy as a continuation of war by other, parallel means This is plainly evident from the nature of Moscow’s proposals for the ‘ new, long-term architecture of indivisible peace and security’ These proposals have little in common with the security system outlined in the Helsinki Final Act (1975). Unlike the principles set out in the declaration signed by 41 states at the European Political Community meeting in Dublin last Thursday, which actually do mirror the original Helsinki ‘decalogue’, Russia’s demands reflect a desire to carve up the continent in the spirit of Yalta. As reported, the demands the Russians made in Abu Dhabi concerning the future European security architecture echo those contained in the draft treaties on European security that Russia proposed in December 2021. NATO must not expand further, and must withdraw its military personnel and infrastructure from allied territory, reverting to its 1997 military posture. Thanks to this gesture of benevolence from Moscow, Central and Eastern Europeans could remain in NATO, but the Alliance could do nothing to defend them. The.

Engineering AI Discover

Engineering AI Discover. The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan , Peng Ren , Gary Tang , Itay Teller , Atif Faheem , Nipun Kumar , Donnie De Boer , Eduardo Lundgren , Matteo Rinaldi , Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover , a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way. Why an intelligence layer? . Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer. The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design: Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not b.

IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems

IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems. Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot. The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter Mc Mahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in Mc Mahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? . Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a ma.

Tina Fordham on Trump's pursuit of a legacy, the Iran war and the race to shape the world after 2028

Tina Fordham on Trump's pursuit of a legacy, the Iran war and the race to shape the world after 2028. The war between the US and Iran has exposed the limits of American military power and raised difficult questions about what comes next for the Middle East. For US President Donald Trump, the challenge is finding a way out of a conflict that has weakened Iran but left the region facing an uncertain future. Geostrategist, author and adviser Tina Fordham believes the consequences will extend far beyond the Strait of Hormuz, with the conflict potentially reshaping political and economic relationships across the region and beyond. In this episode of The Inside Brief , Ms Fordham joins Manus Cranny to discuss Mr Trump's approach to power after his Republican Party's midterm election defeat, why he could double down on military pressure rather than retreat, and how Iran may be calculating that it can outlast the US. In her book Mad World: A Geostrategy Survival Guide for Leaders , Ms Fordham examines the changing role of the US in global security. She explains what this means for the UAE and wider Gulf, and why greater regional co-operation could become increasingly important. Looking beyond the immediate conflict, Ms Fordham explores how Mr Trump's pursuit of a legacy, the question of his successor and the ambitions of leaders including China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are shaping a world in which power is increasingly concentrated, but little thought is given to what comes after. She also reflects on her career as a political risk analyst on Wall Street, and why understanding political motivations is just as important as economic data when making business decisions, something she says the Middle East has long recognised. The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on You Tube , Apple Podcasts , Spotify and other major platforms. .

Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual

Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual. Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. After reporting strong third-quarter numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress (who has been Nvidia’s CFO since 2013) kept the call focused on Nvidia’s immediate business concerns. Analysts wanted to know what the company would say about the succession plan after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race. Most of the salient information about Huang was given at the front of the call by Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair of the board. Jones said Nvidia doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO, providing a clapback to the growing contingent on social media lobbying for the ousted CEO’s return. Jones said the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles is handling the search for a new CEO, but that Nvidia is looking at both internal and external candidates for the job. “The board is acting deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees and investors,” Jones said. “With that we will take no further questions about the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.” The numbers Kress then took over the call and kept things focused on Nvidia’s numbers. Kress has run Nvidia’s earnings calls for years, but always alongside Huang, who set the company’s vision and did much of its dealmaking with customers and partners. Today her main job was to report the quarterly numbers, and convince investors that the world’s most important AI chip company can run without its founder. The numbers, at least, are good. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal third quarter, well above Wall Street’s roughly $109 billion forecast, and projected $130 billion for the current quarter. Investors expected a beat. People’s AI secrets raise questions about the use of chatbots in personal life. A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets. Olivia Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.” Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages : “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had Chat GPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.” “I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.” Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway. As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows? . Some use AI to write personal messages, even if they feel guilty about it As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn’t. “Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.” Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK. Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy. He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said. “What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said. How to know when it’s not OK to use AI Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s meta LAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it’s not. She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it?
